readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unrude''' (un-röd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unrude, unruide, unride, ounride''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (in defs. 2 and 3 intensive) + ''rude.''] '''1.''' Not rude; polished; cultivated. ''Herrick,'' Hesperides, p. 156.—'''2†.''' Excessively rude. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|See how the ''unrude'' rascal backbites him!
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Every Man out of his Humour, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3†.''' Cruel; monstrous.

'''unruffle''' (un-ruf′l), ''v. i.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''ruffle''<sup>1</sup>.] To cease from being ruffled or agitated; subside to smoothness. ''Dryden,'' Æneid, i. 210.

'''unruffled''' (un-ruf′ld), ''a.'' Calm; tranquil; not agitated; not disturbed: as, an ''unruffled'' temper.
{{smaller block|The ''unruffled'' bosom of the stream. {{right|''Hawthorne.''}}}}

'''unruinable''' (un-rö′in-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being ruined or destroyed. ''Watts,'' Remnants of Time, ix. [Rare.]

'''unruinate†''' (un-rö′i-nāt), ''a.'' Not brought to ruin; not in ruins. ''Bp. Hall,'' Apol. against Brownists, § 30. [Rare.]

'''unruined''' (un-rö′ind), ''a.'' Not ruined; not destroyed. ''Bp. Hall,'' Balm of Gilead, § 10. [Rare.]

'''unruled''' (un-röld′), ''a.'' Not ruled. {{smaller|(''a'') Not governed; not directed by superior power or authority. ''Spenser,'' State of Ireland. (''b''†) Unruly. ''Fabyan.'' (''c'') Not marked, by means of a rule or other contrivance, with lines: as, ''unruled'' paper.}}

'''unrulily''' (un-rö′li-li), ''adv.'' In an unruly manner; lawlessly. ''Sir J. Cheke,'' Hurt of Sedition.

'''unruliment†''' (un-rö′li-mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''unruly'' + ''-ment.''] Unruliness. ''Spenser,'' F. Q., IV. ix. 23.

'''unruliness''' (un-rö′li-nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being unruly; disregard of restraint; turbulence: as, the ''unruliness'' of men or of their
readings.c1s2:
passions. ''South'', Sermons.

'''unruly''' (un-rö′li), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ruly''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''disruly''.] Disposed to resist rule or lawful restraint, or to violate laws laid down; lawless; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; disorderly; tumultuous: as, an ''unruly'' child.
{{smaller block|The tongue can no man tame; it is an ''unruly'' evil.
{{right|Jas. iii. 8.}}
<poem>An out-law was this Robin Hood,
His life free and ''unruly''.</poem>
{{right|''In Sherwood livde stout Robin Hood'' (Child’s Ballads, [V. 434).}}}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''unruly†''' (un-rö′li), ''adv.'' [< ''unruly'', ''a.''] Not according to rule; irregularly.

'''unrumple''' (un-rum′pl), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''rumple.''] To free from rumples; spread or lay even. ''Addison'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics, iv.

'''unsacrament''' (un-sak′ra-ment), ''v. t.'' To deprive of sacramental character. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The profaneness of a bad man administering it doth ''unsacrament'' baptism itself.
{{right|''Fuller'', Holy and Profane State, v. 11.}}}}

'''unsad†''' (un-sad′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unsad''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sad.''] Lacking in seriousness; unsettled; unsteady.
{{smaller block|O stormy peple! ''unsad'' and ever untrewe.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 939.}}}}

'''unsadden†''' (un-sad′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''sadden.''] To relieve from sadness. ''Whitlock'', Manners of Eng. People, p. 483.

'''unsaddle''' (un-sad′l), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''saddle.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To strip of a saddle; take the saddle from: as, to ''unsaddle'' a horse.—'''2.''' To cause to dismount or fall from a saddle; unhorse.
{{smaller block|If I believe a fair speaker, I have comfort a little while, though he deceive me, but a froward and peremptory refuser ''unsaddles'' me at first. {{right|''Donne'', Sermons, xvi.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take the saddle from a horse: as, we ''unsaddled'' for an hour’s rest.

'''unsadness''' (un-sad′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unsadnesse''; < ''unsad'' + ''-ness.''] Infirmity; lack of steadiness; weakness. ''Wyclif.''

'''unsafe''' (un-sāf′), ''a.'' Not safe, in any sense.
{{smaller block|No incredulous or ''unsafe'' circumstance.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 88.}}}}
readings.c1s4:
¶
'''unsafely''' (un-sāf′li), ''adv.'' Not safely. ''Dryden'', Eleonora.

'''unsafeness''' (un-sāf′nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsafe.

'''unsafety''' (un-sāf′ti), ''n.'' The state of being unsafe; exposure to danger; insecurity; risk. ''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, iv. 7.

'''unsage†''' (un-sāj′), ''a.'' Not sage or wise; foolish. ''Hudson'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Judith, v. 305. (''Davies.'')

'''unsaid''' (un-sed′), ''a.'' Not said; not spoken; not uttered: as, ''unsaid'' words. ''Dryden'', Cock and Fox, l. 467.

'''unsailable''' (un-sā′la-bl), ''a.'' Not sailable; not navigable. ''May'', tr. of Lucan’s Pharsalia, v.

'''unsaint†''' (un-sānt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''saint''<sup>1</sup>.] To deprive of saintship; divest of saintly character; deny sanctity to. ''South'', Sermons.

'''unsaintly''' (un-sānt′li), ''a.'' Not like a saint; unholy. ''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unsalability''' (un-sā-la̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' Unsalableness. ''Athenæum'', No. 3281, p. 352. Also spelled ''unsaleability''.

'''unsalable''' (un-sā′la̤-bl), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Not salable; not in demand; not meeting a ready sale: as, ''unsalable'' goods.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which is unsalable or cannot be sold.

Also spelled ''unsaleable''.

'''unsalableness''' (un-sā′la̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsalable. Also spelled ''unsaleableness''.

'''unsalaried''' (un-sal′a̤-rid), ''a.'' Not provided with or paid a fixed salary: as, an ''unsalaried'' office or official; hence, depending solely on fees.

'''unsalted''' (un-sâl′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not salted; not pickled; fresh; unseasoned: as, ''unsalted'' meat.
{{smaller block|O, your ''unsalted'' fresh foole is your onely man.
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iv. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' Not salt; having fresh waters, as a river.
{{smaller block|And through the green meadow runs, or rather lounges, a gentle, ''unsalted'' stream, like an English river, licking its grassy margin with a sort of bovine placidity and contentment.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson, p. 70.}}}}

'''unsaluted''' (un-sa-lū′ted), ''a.'' Not saluted; not greeted. ''Shak.'', Cor., v. 3. 50.

'''unsalvable''' (un-sal′va̤-bl), ''a.'' Without capacity of being saved; not savable.
{{smaller block|However, I hope there is still a church in England alive; or else we were all in a sad, yea, in an ''unsalvable'' condition. ''Fuller'', Appeal of Injured Innocence, ii. 102. (''Hall.'')}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unsanctification''' (un-sangk″ti-fi-kā′shọn), ''n.'' The state or character of being unsanctified. ''Coleridge.''

'''unsanctified''' (un-sangk′ti-fīd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not sanctified; unholy; profane. ''V. Knox'', Winter Evenings, xxviii.—'''2.''' Not consecrated. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1. 252.

'''unsanguine''' (un-sang′gwin), ''a.'' Not sanguine; not ardent, animated, or hopeful. ''Young'', The Ocean.

'''unsanitary''' (un-san′i-tā-ri), ''a.'' Not sanitary; unhealthy; not designed or fitted to secure health. ''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xxiii.

'''unsaponifiable''' (un-sā-pon′i-fī-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of saponification.

'''unsapped''' (un-sapt′), ''a.'' Not sapped; not undermined or secretly attacked. ''Sterne.''

'''unsatiability†''' (un-sā″shiạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' Unsatiableness.

'''unsatiable''' (un-sā′shiạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being satiated or appeased; insatiable. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.

'''unsatiableness''' (un-sā′shiạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being insatiable; insatiability; insatiableness.

'''unsatiably''' (un-sā′shiạ-bli), ''adv.'' Insatiably. [Rare.]

'''unsatiate†''' (un-sā′shiāt), ''a.'' Insatiate. ''Dr. H. More'', Sleep of the Soul, iii. 11.

'''unsatisfaction†''' (un-sat-is-fak′shọn), ''n.'' Dissatisfaction. ''Bp. Hall'', Of Contentation.

'''unsatisfactorily''' (un-sat-is-fak′tọ̄-ri-li), ''adv.'' In an unsatisfactory manner. ''Amer. Jour. Archæol.'', VI. 516.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unsatisfactoriness''' (un-sat-is-fak′tọ̄-ri-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsatisfactory; failure to give satisfaction. ''Boyle'', Works, III. Pref.

'''unsatisfactory''' (un-sat-is-fak′tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not satisfactory; not satisfying; not giving satisfaction. ''Sir T. Browne'', Letter to a Friend.

'''unsatisfiable''' (un-sat′is-fī-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being satisfied: as, ''unsatisfiable'' passions. ''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 74.

'''unsatisfied''' (un-sat′is-fīd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not satisfied; not gratified to the full: as, ''unsatisfied'' appetites or desires. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iv. 2. 55. —'''2.''' Not content; not pleased; dissatisfied. [Now rare.]
{{smaller block|Divers of the magistrates being ''unsatisfied'' with this verdict, . . . the defendants at the next court brought a review. {{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 299.}}}}
'''3.''' Not fully informed; not convinced or fully persuaded.
{{smaller block|Whatsoever the Bishops were, it seems they themselves were ''unsatisfi’d'' in matters of Religion.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
'''4.''' Not paid; unpaid; undischarged: as, an ''unsatisfied'' bill or account. ''Shak.'', L. L. L., ii. 1. 139.

'''unsatisfiedness''' (un-sat′is-fīd-nes), ''n.'' The state of being dissatisfied or discontented. ''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 31.

'''unsatisfying''' (un-sat′is-fī-ing), ''a.'' Not satisfying or affording full gratification of appetite or desire; not giving content; not convincing the mind. ''Addison.''
readings.c3s2:
¶

'''unscalable''' (un-skā′la-bl), ''a.'' Not to be scaled; incapable of being climbed or mounted. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 1. 20. Also ''unscaleable.''
{{smaller block|Far below, out of sight over the edge, lay the torrent; ''unscalable'' the cliff rose above. ''The Atlantic'', LXVII. 376.}}

'''unscale''' (un-skāl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''scale''<sup>1</sup>.] To remove scales from; divest of scales.
{{smaller block|''Unscaling'' her long-abused sight. ''Milton'', Areopagitica.}}

'''unscaly''' (un-skā′li), ''a.'' Not scaly; having no scales. ''Gay'', Trivia, ii. 416.

'''unscanned''' (un-skand′), ''a.'' Not scanned; not measured; not computed. ''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 313.

'''unscapable†''' (un-skā′pa̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be escaped.

'''unscarred''' (un-skärd′), ''a.'' Not marked with scars; hence, unwounded; unhurt: as, an ''unscarred'' veteran. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 209.

'''unscathed''' (un-skāᴛ̵ʜd′), ''a.'' Uninjured. ''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.

'''unsceptered, unsceptred''' (un-sep′tėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no scepter or royal authority.—'''2.''' Deprived of a scepter; unkinged: as, the ''unsceptered'' Lear. ''Poetry of Antijacobin'', p. 138. (''Davies.'')

'''unscholar†''' (un-skol′är), ''n.'' One who is not a scholar; an illiterate person. ''Ascham'', Toxophilus, p. 38. (''Davies.'')

'''unschooled''' (un-sköld′), ''a.'' Not schooled; not taught; not educated; illiterate; not developed by study. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2. 97.

'''unscience†''' (un-sī′ens), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unscience''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''science''.] Lack of knowledge; igno-
readings.c3s3:
rance.

{{smaller block|If that any wyht weene a thing to ben oother weyes thanne it is, it is nat oonly ''unscience'' but it is deceyvable opynyon.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 3.}}}}

'''unscissored''' (un-siz′o̤rd), ''a.'' Not cut with scissors; not sheared. ''Shak.'', Pericles, iii. 3. 29.

'''unscottify''' (un-skot′i-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unscottified'', ppr. ''unscottifying''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''Scottify''.] To deprive of Scotch characteristics. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Examples of great power in Scottish phraseology, . . . which lose their charm altogether when ''unscottified''.
{{right|''E. B. Ramsey'', Scottish Life and Character, p. 91.}}}}

'''unscoured''' (un-skourd′), ''a.'' Not scoured; not cleaned by rubbing: as, ''unscoured'' armor; ''unscoured'' wool. ''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 171.

'''unscratched''' (un-skracht′), ''a.'' Not scratched; not torn. ''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 225.

'''unscreened''' (un-skrēnd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not screened; not covered; not sheltered; not protected. ''Boyle.''—'''2.''' Not passed through a screen; not sifted: as, ''unscreened'' coal.

'''unscrew''' (un-skrö′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''screw''<sup>1</sup>.] To draw the screws from; unfasten by taking out screws; also, to loosen (a screw) by turning it so as to withdraw it: often used figuratively.

{{smaller block|<poem>I should curse my fortune,
Even at the highest, to be made the gin
To ''unscrew'' a mother’s love unto her son.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another?)'', Queen of Corinth, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Divers of the magistrates being ''unsatisfied'' with this verdict, . . . the defendants at the next court brought a review. {{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 299.}}}}
'''3.''' Not fully informed; not convinced or fully persuaded.
{{smaller block|Whatsoever the Bishops were, it seems they themselves were ''unsatisfi’d'' in matters of Religion.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
'''4.''' Not paid; unpaid; undischarged: as, an ''unsatisfied'' bill or account. ''Shak.'', L. L. L., ii. 1. 139.

'''unsatisfiedness''' (un-sat′is-fīd-nes), ''n.'' The state of being dissatisfied or discontented. ''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 31.

'''unsatisfying''' (un-sat′is-fī-ing), ''a.'' Not satisfying or affording full gratification of appetite or desire; not giving content; not convincing the mind. ''Addison.''

'''unsatisfyingness''' (un-sat′is-fī-ing-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unsatisfying or not gratifying to the full. ''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 859.

'''unsaturated''' (un-sat̮′ṳ̄-rā-ted), ''a.'' Not saturated.
{{smaller block|The majority of “alloisomerides” are compounds containing ''unsaturated'' carbon. {{right|''Nature'', XXXIX. 119.}}}}

'''unsaturation''' (un-sat̮-ṳ̄-rā′shọn), ''n.'' The state of being unsaturated.

'''unsavorily, unsavourily''' (un-sā′vo̤r-i-li), ''adv.'' In an unsavory manner. ''Milton'', Animadversions.

'''unsavoriness, unsavouriness''' (un-sā′vo̤r-i-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unsavory.

'''unsavory, unsavoury''' (un-sā′vo̤r-i), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not savory; tasteless; insipid. Job vi. 6.—'''2.''' Disagreeable to the taste or smell. ''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 3. 31.—'''3.''' Unpleasing; offensive, intellectually or morally; disagreeable. ''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.
{{smaller block|Thou hast the most ''unsavoury'' similes. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2. 89.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn. 2.''' Unpalatable, ill-flavored, stale.—'''3.''' Disgusting, nauseous.}}

'''unsay''' (un-sā′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unsaid'', ppr. ''unsaying''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''say''<sup>1</sup>.] To recant or recall after having been said; retract; take back: as, to ''unsay'' one’s words.
{{smaller block|Scorns to ''unsay'' what once it hath delivered. {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II. iv. 1. 9.}}
<poem>Retire a while,
Whilst I ''unsay'' myself unto the Duke,
And cast out that ill spirit I have possess’d him with.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, iii. 1.}}}}

'''unscalable''' (un-skā′la-bl), ''a.'' Not to be scaled; incapable of being climbed or mounted. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 1. 20. Also ''unscaleable.''
{{smaller block|Far below, out of sight over the edge, lay the torrent; ''unscalable'' the cliff rose above. ''The Atlantic'', LXVII. 376.}}

'''unscale''' (un-skāl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''scale''<sup>1</sup>.] To remove scales from; divest of scales.
{{smaller block|''Unscaling'' her long-abused sight. ''Milton'', Areopagitica.}}

'''unscaly''' (un-skā′li), ''a.'' Not scaly; having no scales. ''Gay'', Trivia, ii. 416.

'''unscanned''' (un-skand′), ''a.'' Not scanned; not measured; not computed. ''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 313.

'''unscapable†''' (un-skā′pa̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be escaped.

'''unscarred''' (un-skärd′), ''a.'' Not marked with scars; hence, unwounded; unhurt: as, an ''unscarred'' veteran. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 209.

'''unscathed''' (un-skāᴛ̵ʜd′), ''a.'' Uninjured. ''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.

'''unsceptered, unsceptred''' (un-sep′tėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no scepter or royal authority.—'''2.''' Deprived of a scepter; unkinged: as, the ''unsceptered'' Lear. ''Poetry of Antijacobin'', p. 138. (''Davies.'')

'''unscholar†''' (un-skol′är), ''n.'' One who is not a scholar; an illiterate person. ''Ascham'', Toxophilus, p. 38. (''Davies.'')

'''unschooled''' (un-sköld′), ''a.'' Not schooled; not taught; not educated; illiterate; not developed by study. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2. 97.

'''unscience†''' (un-sī′ens), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unscience''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''science''.] Lack of knowledge; ignorance.

{{smaller block|If that any wyht weene a thing to ben oother weyes thanne it is, it is nat oonly ''unscience'' but it is deceyvable opynyon.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 3.}}}}

'''unscissored''' (un-siz′o̤rd), ''a.'' Not cut with scissors; not sheared. ''Shak.'', Pericles, iii. 3. 29.

'''unscottify''' (un-skot′i-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unscottified'', ppr. ''unscottifying''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''Scottify''.] To deprive of Scotch characteristics. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Examples of great power in Scottish phraseology, . . . which lose their charm altogether when ''unscottified''.
{{right|''E. B. Ramsey'', Scottish Life and Character, p. 91.}}}}

'''unscoured''' (un-skourd′), ''a.'' Not scoured; not cleaned by rubbing: as, ''unscoured'' armor; ''unscoured'' wool. ''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 171.

'''unscratched''' (un-skracht′), ''a.'' Not scratched; not torn. ''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 225.

'''unscreened''' (un-skrēnd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not screened; not covered; not sheltered; not protected. ''Boyle.''—'''2.''' Not passed through a screen; not sifted: as, ''unscreened'' coal.

'''unscrew''' (un-skrö′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''screw''<sup>1</sup>.] To draw the screws from; unfasten by taking out screws; also, to loosen (a screw) by turning it so as to withdraw it: often used figuratively.

<poem>I should curse my fortune,
Even at the highest, to be made the gin
To ''unscrew'' a mother’s love unto her son.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher (and another?)'', Queen of Corinth, iii. 1.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
